LinearMask-GS

LinearMask-GS: Stable-Mask Importance Pruning for Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting

Donghun Ryu    Minhyeok Lee
Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis but produces millions of primitives through adaptive densification, leading to significant storage overhead. Learned-mask pruning methods such as LP-3DGS address this by assigning each Gaussian a learnable mask to identify and prune redundant primitives. However, we identify a limitation of this paradigm: the steep slope of the Gumbel-Sigmoid activation drives mask values to the extremes within the short mask-training window, before the importance ranking has stabilized, producing a sharply bimodal distribution from which that ranking can no longer be reliably recovered. We propose LinearMask-GS, which replaces Gumbel-Sigmoid with a linear increment activation that keeps mask values in a mid-confidence regime throughout mask training, producing a stable, unimodal mask distribution whose ranking tracks importance. On Mip-NeRF 360, our method achieves 3.6×3.6\times and 1.6×1.6\times Gaussian reductions over 3DGS and LP-3DGS, respectively, while maintaining or improving rendering quality. For outdoor scenes, it yields a 1.6×1.6\times reduction (from 2.18M to 1.36M) with notable gains in PSNR (+0.38 dB), SSIM (+0.025), and LPIPS (-0.029).

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] has become a leading representation for novel view synthesis, achieving high-fidelity real-time rendering by encoding scenes as millions of explicit Gaussian primitives. Despite this rendering efficiency, the adaptive densification process routinely produces millions of primitives, and a standard outdoor scene in Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al.(2022)Barron, Mildenhall, Verbin, Srinivasan, and Hedman] can exceed 1GB in storage [Xie et al.(2024)Xie, Zhang, Tang, Bai, Lu, Ge, and Wang], limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices.

Prior methods reduce this overhead either by compressing per-Gaussian attributes [Niedermayr et al.(2024)Niedermayr, Stumpfegger, and Westermann, Lee et al.(2024)Lee, Rho, Sun, Ko, and Park, Xie et al.(2024)Xie, Zhang, Tang, Bai, Lu, Ge, and Wang], which leaves the primitive count and rasterization cost unchanged, or by pruning low-importance Gaussians post hoc [Fan et al.(2024)Fan, Wang, Wen, Zhu, Xu, and Wang, Fang and Wang(2024), Niemeyer et al.(2025)Niemeyer, Manhardt, Rakotosaona, Oechsle, Duckworth, Gosula, Tateno, Bates, Kaeser, and Tombari], which lacks feedback from scene optimization and often discards geometrically essential primitives, yielding suboptimal quality–compression trade-offs (Sec. 2).

LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan] addresses this by learning a per-Gaussian soft mask jointly with the scene, using a Gumbel-Sigmoid activation so the mask can be optimized end-to-end and then thresholded into a hard keep/prune decision. This couples pruning with scene optimization, but we observe that the soft mask it produces is, by the time pruning happens, no longer a faithful summary of importance.

The learned mask saturates before importance ranking stabilizes. The Gumbel-Sigmoid activation used in LP-3DGS is steep: small changes in the underlying parameter swing the mask all the way to 00 or 11, so the mask collapses to these two extreme values long before the per-Gaussian importance signal has settled into a meaningful ranking. This saturation is a property of the activation itself rather than of the brevity of the mask-training window: with the pruning point held fixed, extending the window monotonically worsens saturation (Sec. 3.3). As shown in Fig. 1(a, b), the resulting distribution is sharply two-peaked (i.e., bimodal), with almost every value pinned to either 00 or 11, and which side a Gaussian lands on is largely an artifact of early optimization rather than its true contribution to the rendered image. Pruning a distribution like this is unreliable: the ranking induced by ψi\psi_{i} reflects the side of saturation more than the magnitude of importance, and the standard remedy of enforcing a minimum-survival ratio [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan] prevents geometry collapse without addressing this underlying cause.

To address this, we propose LinearMask-GS, a learned-mask pruning framework that targets the cause of this brittleness by changing how the mask is shaped during training. We replace Gumbel-Sigmoid with a linear increment activation whose gentle slope keeps mask values in the middle of the [0,1][0,1] range, a mid-confidence regime, throughout the mask-training window, rather than letting them saturate at 00 or 11. The resulting distribution (Fig. 1(c, d)) is unimodal, so the relative order of mask values is preserved rather than collapsed onto 00 and 11, and hard pruning therefore operates on a stable ranking rather than a two-peaked one. Because the activation only changes how the mask is shaped, not how it is applied, LinearMask-GS integrates without architectural modifications into a range of Gaussian-based backbones, including 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.], 2DGS [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao], DropGaussian [Park et al.(2025)Park, Ryu, and Kim], Octree-GS [Ren et al.(2024)Ren, Jiang, Lu, Yu, Xu, Ni, and Dai], and FastGS [Ren et al.(2025)Ren, Wen, Fang, and Lu].

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify that the steep activation of learned-mask pruning saturates the soft mask at 00 or 11 before the importance ranking stabilizes, a failure mode that longer mask-training windows worsen rather than fix, yielding a two-peaked distribution from which that ranking can no longer be reliably recovered.

  • •

    We propose the linear increment masking activation, whose gentle slope keeps mask values away from the boundaries and yields a unimodal distribution whose ranking is preserved rather than collapsed, on which a simple top-ρ​N\rho N selection gives a reliable hard-pruning decision.

  • •

    On Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, LinearMask-GS achieves better quality–compression trade-offs than existing learned-mask and pruning baselines on 3DGS, and the same masking module transfers without modification to 2DGS, DropGaussian, Octree-GS, and FastGS.

2 Related Work

2.1 Novel View Synthesis

While Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al.(2021)Mildenhall, Srinivasan, Tancik, Barron, Ramamoorthi, and Ng, Barron et al.(2022)Barron, Mildenhall, Verbin, Srinivasan, and Hedman, Müller et al.(2022)Müller, Evans, Schied, and Keller] achieve high-quality novel view synthesis, dense ray marching limits their real-time application. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] overcomes this by combining explicit 3D Gaussian primitives with a fast tile-based rasterizer. Subsequent methods have extended this framework to improve anti-aliasing [Yu et al.(2024)Yu, Chen, Huang, Sattler, and Geiger], scaling [Lu et al.(2024)Lu, Yu, Xu, Xiangli, Wang, Lin, and Dai], and surface reconstruction via 2D oriented disks (2DGS) [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao]. Despite these advances, adaptive densification leaves all of them with millions of primitives and the attendant memory and storage overhead (Sec. 1).

2.2 Gaussian Compression and Pruning

To reduce storage costs without modifying the number of Gaussians, several works compress per-Gaussian attributes via vector quantization, residual quantization of color and rotation, or post-training codecs based on entropy coding and region-adaptive hierarchical transforms [Niedermayr et al.(2024)Niedermayr, Stumpfegger, and Westermann, Girish et al.(2024)Girish, Gupta, and Shrivastava, Lee et al.(2024)Lee, Rho, Sun, Ko, and Park, Xie et al.(2024)Xie, Zhang, Tang, Bai, Lu, Ge, and Wang]. While effective at reducing per-attribute storage, these methods leave the total number of Gaussian primitives unchanged and thus do not alleviate rasterization time complexity.

Pruning methods directly reduce the Gaussian count by removing redundant primitives. The original 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] periodically culls Gaussians with low opacity or excessively large scale as part of adaptive density control. LightGaussian [Fan et al.(2024)Fan, Wang, Wen, Zhu, Xu, and Wang] prunes low-scoring primitives by a heuristic significance score, and Mini-Splatting [Fang and Wang(2024)] reorganizes Gaussian positions via a densification-and-sampling pipeline. RadSplat [Niemeyer et al.(2025)Niemeyer, Manhardt, Rakotosaona, Oechsle, Duckworth, Gosula, Tateno, Bates, Kaeser, and Tombari] shows that taking the per-view maximum blending weight as the importance score yields a more stable and discriminative signal than summation-based alternatives. Despite their utility, these heuristic methods rely on manually tuned thresholds and treat pruning as a post-hoc step decoupled from scene geometry optimization, leading to accidental removal of geometrically essential primitives. Our method overcomes these limitations by coupling pruning decisions directly with scene reconstruction through learned importance masks.

2.3 Differentiable Gaussian Pruning

To overcome the limitations of manual thresholding, recent work introduces end-to-end differentiable masking frameworks. LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan] assigns a learnable binary mask to each Gaussian and jointly optimizes masks alongside scene parameters, accumulating importance scores by summing pixel-level blending weights and binarizing them through a Gumbel-Sigmoid activation. Taming-3DGS [Mallick et al.(2024)Mallick, Goel, Kerbl, Steinberger, Carrasco, and De La Torre] and Reduced-3DGS [Papantonakis et al.(2024)Papantonakis, Kopanas, Kerbl, Lanvin, and Drettakis] extend this paradigm with explicit Gaussian count budgets and attribute quantization, respectively, targeting deployment on resource-limited hardware.

While these methods demonstrate the benefit of jointly learning pruning decisions and scene geometry, they inherit summation-based score inflation and, more fundamentally, the premature saturation of the steep Gumbel-Sigmoid mask; our approach addresses both with max-pooling aggregation and a linear-increment activation that restores a stable ranking for the top-ρ​N\rho N rule (Secs. 3.2–3.3).

3 Method

We propose a differentiable pruning framework that jointly optimizes per-Gaussian mask parameters alongside scene geometry, compressing Gaussian-based representations while largely preserving PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. We develop it on 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] and 2DGS [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao], and show that it transfers without modification to other backbones (Sec. 4).

After an initial geometric warm-up phase using the standard Gaussian Splatting pipeline, the framework proceeds in three stages: (1) computing a max-pooled importance score SiS_{i} for each primitive to evaluate view-count-invariant relevance (Sec. 3.2), (2) jointly optimizing per-Gaussian learnable mask parameters with the proposed linear increment activation, which keeps mask values away from 00 and 11 throughout the mask-training window (Sec. 3.3), and (3) applying a hard-pruning rule that retains the top-ρ​N\rho N Gaussians ranked by ψi\psi_{i}, where ρ\rho is the minimum-survival ratio, followed by fine-tuning of the remaining scene (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries

3D Gaussian Splatting.

3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] represents a scene as a set of NN anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Each Gaussian ii is parameterized by a mean position 𝝁i∈ℝ3\boldsymbol{\mu}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, a covariance matrix 𝚺i=𝐑i​𝐒i​𝐒i⊤​𝐑i⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{i}^{\top} (decomposed into a rotation matrix 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i} and a diagonal scaling matrix 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i}), an opacity logit oi∈ℝo_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic coefficients encoding view-dependent color 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i}.

Primitives are projected and depth-sorted to compute color 𝐂\mathbf{C} via front-to-back alpha compositing:

𝐂=∑i=1N𝐜i​αi​∏j<i(1−αj),αi=σ⁡(oi)⋅exp⁡(−12​𝐝⊤​𝚺i,2D−1​𝐝),\mathbf{C}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{c}_{i}\,\alpha_{i}\prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_{j}),\quad\alpha_{i}=\sigma(o_{i})\cdot\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}_{i,\text{2D}}\mathbf{d}\right), (1)

Here, 𝐝\mathbf{d} is the 2D offset to the projected center, 𝚺i,2D\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i,\text{2D}} is the covariance, and σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid. The per-Gaussian blending weight at pixel 𝐩\mathbf{p} under viewpoint kk is:

wik,𝐩=αik,𝐩​∏j<i(1−αjk,𝐩),w_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}=\alpha_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}\prod_{j<i}(1-\alpha_{j}^{k,\mathbf{p}}), (2)

which measures the fractional contribution of Gaussian ii to the rendered pixel color.

2D Gaussian Splatting.

2DGS [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao] replaces 3D ellipsoids with oriented 2D disk primitives embedded in 3D space, improving multi-view geometric consistency. Its compositing follows the same front-to-back formulation as Eq. (1) (with an explicit ray-splat intersection), and the blending weight wik,𝐩w_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}} retains the form of Eq. (2), providing a unified interface for importance score computation across both representations.

3.2 Importance Score via Max-Pooling

A key design choice in differentiable Gaussian pruning is how to aggregate per-pixel, per-view blending weights into a single scalar importance score SiS_{i} for each Gaussian. Several prior methods adopt summation-based aggregation [Fang and Wang(2024), Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan]:

Sisum=∑k=1K∑𝐩wik,𝐩,S_{i}^{\text{sum}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{\mathbf{p}}w_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}, (3)

where the sum runs over all KK training viewpoints and all pixels 𝐩\mathbf{p}. This formulation inflates scores for Gaussians in densely observed regions, reducing the discriminability of the importance signal.

To address this, we adopt the max-pooling aggregation proposed by RadSplat [Niemeyer et al.(2025)Niemeyer, Manhardt, Rakotosaona, Oechsle, Duckworth, Gosula, Tateno, Bates, Kaeser, and Tombari] to compute importance scores over all training views:

Si=maxk∈{1,…,K}⁡(max𝐩⁡wik,𝐩).S_{i}=\max_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}\Bigl(\max_{\mathbf{p}}w_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}\Bigr). (4)

This captures the peak contribution of a Gaussian in its most favorable viewpoint, providing a view-count-invariant measure of geometric relevance. A Gaussian that contributes strongly to at least one view retains a high score regardless of how many views overlap the same region, effectively mitigating the view-count inflation associated with Eq. (3).

3.3 Differentiable Pruning via Linear Increment Masking

Mask formulation.

We assign each Gaussian ii a learnable scalar parameter mi∈ℝm_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, initialized to 1 to ensure all primitives start fully visible and participate equally in the initial geometric optimization. The per-Gaussian mask value is:

ψi=f⁡(mi⋅Si),\psi_{i}=f(m_{i}\cdot S_{i}), (5)

where f:ℝ→[0,1]f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] is the mask activation and SiS_{i} is the importance score from Eq. (4). During rendering, the opacity of each Gaussian is modulated as:

α~ik,𝐩=ψi⋅αik,𝐩,\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}=\psi_{i}\cdot\alpha_{i}^{k,\mathbf{p}}, (6)

so that Gaussians with ψi≈0\psi_{i}\approx 0 are differentiably suppressed while gradients flow through both mim_{i} and the scene parameters concurrently.

Linear increment activation.

LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan] employs Gumbel-Sigmoid as ff:

fGS​(x)=11+exp⁡(−log⁡(x)+g0−g1t),g0,g1∼Gumbel⁡(0,1),f_{\text{GS}}(x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log(x)+g_{0}-g_{1}}{t}\right)},\quad g_{0},g_{1}\sim\mathrm{Gumbel}(0,1), (7)

where tt is the temperature parameter. The steep slope of fGSf_{\text{GS}} near its midpoint causes a small change in mi⋅Sim_{i}\cdot S_{i} to produce a large change in ψi\psi_{i}, so mask outputs are pushed toward 00 or 11 within the short mask-training window before the importance score SiS_{i} has stabilized. As shown in Fig. 1(a, b), this yields a two-peaked ψi\psi_{i} distribution pinned at 00 and 11. We refer to this behavior as mask instability: which extreme each mask lands on reflects an artifact of early optimization more than the magnitude of SiS_{i} itself. This instability stems from the activation’s steepness rather than from the window length: with the pruning point fixed at iteration 20k, extending the Gumbel-Sigmoid mask window from 500500 to 2,5002{,}500 and 5,0005{,}000 iterations monotonically increases the saturated fraction (51.1%→54.8%→56.2%51.1\%\to 54.8\%\to 56.2\% on three scenes) while PSNR plateaus, whereas the linear ranking is robust to window placement (window starts of 15k/17.5k/19.5k change final PSNR by ≤0.14\leq 0.14 dB); see Sec. 4 of the supplementary material.

We therefore propose the linear increment activation:

fLI​(x,τ)=clip⁡(τ⋅(x−0.5)+0.5, 0, 1),f_{\text{LI}}(x;\,\tau)=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\tau\cdot(x-0.5)+0.5,\;0,\;1\right), (8)

where τ>0\tau>0 is a slope hyperparameter. With a small slope (we use τ=0.1\tau{=}0.1), fLIf_{\text{LI}} has a wide unsaturated range and is monotone-linear in its active interval, so a change in mi⋅Sim_{i}\cdot S_{i} produces a proportionally small change in ψi\psi_{i}. As a result, mask values stay close to the neutral midpoint 0.50.5 throughout mask training and the output distribution remains unimodal and centered away from 00 and 11, as shown in Fig. 1(c, d). We refer to this property as mask stability: because the values stay spread across the mid-range instead of collapsing to a binary indicator, their relative order is preserved rather than compressed onto the saturation points, so ψi\psi_{i} yields a stable ranking for pruning. Quantitatively, across the nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes at iteration 20,00020{,}000, the Linear mask distribution shows 0.00%0.00\% saturation (ψi<0.1\psi_{i}<0.1 or ψi>0.9\psi_{i}>0.9) and 99.99%99.99\% of values lying in the interval [0.3,0.7][0.3,0.7], with a per-Gaussian standard deviation of only 0.0180.018. In contrast, Gumbel-Sigmoid saturates 51.19%51.19\% of mask values and retains only 20.28%20.28\% in [0.3,0.7][0.3,0.7], with a much larger standard deviation of 0.3800.380.

Hard pruning via top-ρ​N\rho N selection.

At the end of mask training, we convert the soft mask values into a hard keep/prune decision. Because the linear-increment activation keeps ψi\psi_{i} unimodal and centered around 0.50.5, the relative order of mask values is preserved rather than compressed onto the saturation points, so ψi\psi_{i} provides a stable ranking. We exploit this by directly retaining the top-ρ​N\rho N Gaussians by ψi\psi_{i}, where ρ=0.30\rho=0.30 is the minimum-survival ratio and NN the total number of Gaussians:

𝒦=top-​ρ​N​ Gaussians ranked by ​ψi.\mathcal{K}=\text{top-}\rho N\text{ Gaussians ranked by }\psi_{i}. (9)

Gaussians in 𝒦\mathcal{K} are retained and the rest are permanently pruned. This rule plays the same role as the minimum-survival ratio in LP-3DGS (bounding the kept fraction to prevent geometry collapse), but because ψi\psi_{i} here is unimodal and its rank tracks importance, the kept set follows the underlying importance ranking instead of the early saturation outcome.

Throughout the mask-training phase, the soft mask value ψi∈[0,1]\psi_{i}\in[0,1] produced by the linear-increment activation is applied directly as an opacity multiplier via Eq. (6), so gradients propagate through both mim_{i} and the scene parameters without hard discretization. The hard-pruning rule of Eq. (9) is applied only once at the end of mask training, as described in Sec. 3.4.

3.4 Training Objective and Schedule

The total training loss combines photometric reconstruction and mask sparsity:

ℒtotal=(1−λD)​ℒ1+λD​(1−SSIM)+λm​ℒmask,\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=(1-\lambda_{D})\,\mathcal{L}_{1}+\lambda_{D}\,(1-\mathrm{SSIM})+\lambda_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\text{mask}}, (10)

where ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} is the pixel-wise ℓ1\ell_{1} loss, SSIM is the structural similarity metric [Wang et al.(2004)Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli], and λD=0.2\lambda_{D}=0.2 follows the default 3DGS setting [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.]. The sparsity term follows LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan]:

ℒmask=1N​∑i=1N|mi|,\mathcal{L}_{\text{mask}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lvert m_{i}\rvert, (11)

which encourages the mask parameters mim_{i} to shrink during training, thereby reducing the corresponding soft mask values after scaling by SiS_{i}. We set λm=5×10−4\lambda_{m}=5\times 10^{-4} and τ=0.1\tau=0.1 for the linear increment activation, using a separate AdamW optimizer [Loshchilov and Hutter(2017)] for {mi}\{m_{i}\} at a learning rate of 5×10−25\times 10^{-2}.

Optimization schedule.

Training proceeds for 30,00030{,}000 iterations in total. For both the 3DGS and 2DGS backbones, we warm up the standard pipeline for 19,50019{,}500 iterations to ensure geometric convergence before activating the mask module. During the subsequent 500500-iteration mask training phase (iterations 19,50019{,}500–20,00020{,}000), the max-pooling importance scores SiS_{i} from Eq. (4) are recomputed every 2020 iterations to reflect ongoing geometric changes. At iteration 20,00020{,}000, we apply the hard-pruning rule of Eq. (9) introduced in Sec. 3.3: the top-ρ​N\rho N Gaussians ranked by ψi\psi_{i} are kept, where ρ\rho is the minimum-survival ratio. We use ρ=0.30\rho=0.30 as the default and study its effect in Sec. 4. The remaining primitives are fine-tuned without the mask loss for the remainder of training.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate LinearMask-GS on three novel view synthesis benchmarks: Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al.(2022)Barron, Mildenhall, Verbin, Srinivasan, and Hedman] (9 scenes), Tanks and Temples [Knapitsch et al.(2017)Knapitsch, Park, Zhou, and Koltun] (2 outdoor scenes), and Deep Blending [Hedman et al.(2018)Hedman, Philip, Price, Frahm, Drettakis, and Brostow] (2 indoor scenes).

Baselines.

We compare LinearMask-GS against generic novel view synthesis and scene representation baselines (Plenoxels [Fridovich-Keil et al.(2022)Fridovich-Keil, Yu, Tancik, Chen, Recht, and Kanazawa], INGP [Müller et al.(2022)Müller, Evans, Schied, and Keller], Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al.(2022)Barron, Mildenhall, Verbin, Srinivasan, and Hedman], 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.], and 2DGS [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao]), as well as 3DGS-based pruning and compression methods (Compact3DGS [Lee et al.(2024)Lee, Rho, Sun, Ko, and Park], LightGaussian [Fan et al.(2024)Fan, Wang, Wen, Zhu, Xu, and Wang], EAGLES [Girish et al.(2024)Girish, Gupta, and Shrivastava], RadSplat [Niemeyer et al.(2025)Niemeyer, Manhardt, Rakotosaona, Oechsle, Duckworth, Gosula, Tateno, Bates, Kaeser, and Tombari], Mini-Splatting [Fang and Wang(2024)], and LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan]). In Table 1, we additionally report a retrained baseline (3DGS∗\text{3DGS}^{*}) to provide a fair comparative reference trained under our identical hardware and schedule. Note that for LP-3DGS, we evaluate its official implementation but apply max-pooling aggregation instead of its original summation-based method. This provides a stronger baseline and ensures a fair comparison by strictly isolating the effect of the mask activation function.

Evaluation metrics.

Rendering quality is assessed via PSNR, SSIM [Wang et al.(2004)Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli], and LPIPS [Zhang et al.(2018)Zhang, Isola, Efros, Shechtman, and Wang]. Compression efficiency is measured by the surviving Gaussian count and storage size (MB).

Implementation details.

We implement LinearMask-GS in PyTorch, building upon the official 3DGS codebase [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.]. The slope τ=0.1\tau{=}0.1 (grid search over {0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5}\{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5\}), minimum-survival ratio ρ=0.30\rho{=}0.30, and mask weight λm=5×10−4\lambda_{m}{=}5\times 10^{-4} are tuned on a held-out set and fixed across all scenes; sensitivity analyses are provided in the supplementary material. Training follows the standard 30,00030{,}000-iteration 3DGS schedule. We train the 3DGS- and 2DGS-backbone runs on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, and the FastGS-backbone run (LinearMask-GS★) on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, following the hardware setup of the FastGS paper [Ren et al.(2025)Ren, Wen, Fang, and Lu]. For a fair wall-clock comparison, the training-time measurements in Table 2 are all collected on a single RTX 4090.

4.2 Main Results

We evaluate LinearMask-GS against scene representation and pruning baselines on three standard benchmarks: Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al.(2022)Barron, Mildenhall, Verbin, Srinivasan, and Hedman], Tanks & Temples [Knapitsch et al.(2017)Knapitsch, Park, Zhou, and Koltun], and Deep Blending [Hedman et al.(2018)Hedman, Philip, Price, Frahm, Drettakis, and Brostow]. For all datasets, we follow the standard evaluation protocol of 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.], where every eighth image is reserved for testing. We report PSNR (dB), SSIM, LPIPS, and the number of Gaussians (M) on all benchmarks, plus FPS and storage (MB) on Mip-NeRF 360 (measured on the same hardware for reproduced methods, and taken from the original papers for literature baselines).

Mip-NeRF 360.

Table 1 summarizes results across all nine scenes against three families of baselines: the original 3DGS backbone with its retrained reference and the LP-3DGS learned-mask parent; compression- and pruning-oriented systems; and recent fast-training pipelines. Compared to the vanilla 3DGS [Kerbl et al.(2023)Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, Drettakis, et al.] backbone, our method reduces the Gaussian count from 3.36M to 0.94M (a 3.6×3.6\times reduction) while improving PSNR from 27.21 to 27.70 dB. Against our primary pruning baseline LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan], LinearMask-GS surpasses it by 0.23 dB in PSNR and 0.0135 in SSIM with 1.6×1.6\times fewer Gaussians, while maintaining comparable rendering speed (591 vs. 588 FPS).

Compared to recent compression methods (HAC [Chen et al.(2024)Chen, Wu, Lin, Harandi, and Cai], HAC++ [Chen et al.(2025a)Chen, Wu, Lin, Harandi, and Cai]) and aggressive pruning baselines (Mini-Splatting [Fang and Wang(2024)], Speedy-Splat [Hanson et al.(2025a)Hanson, Tu, Lin, Singla, Zwicker, and Goldstein]), LinearMask-GS achieves competitive PSNR with substantially fewer Gaussians than compression methods while maintaining higher quality than the most aggressive pruning baselines (see Table 1 for details). For a budget-matched comparison with the most aggressive pruning baseline, we additionally constrain LinearMask-GS★ to Speedy-Splat’s budget of 0.30M Gaussians: over three independent seeds it reaches 27.4027.40 dB / 0.7980.798 / 0.2300.230, versus 26.9126.91 / 0.7810.781 / 0.2950.295 for Speedy-Splat, i.e., better on all three metrics at the same budget, and still ahead at 0.25M (27.0627.06 / 0.7910.791 / 0.2410.241); see Sec. 11 of the supplementary material. Applying LinearMask-GS on the FastGS backbone (LinearMask-GS★, last row), where LinearMask-GS substitutes FastGS’s post-densification VCP module, further compresses the FastGS output from 0.40M to 0.38M Gaussians while improving PSNR by 0.13 dB over FastGS (27.69 vs. 27.56 dB) and reducing storage to 94.89 MB. This indicates that our masking strategy can replace specialized post-densification pruning components in fast-training pipelines while improving rendering quality.

Figure 3 summarizes this advantage through efficiency metrics across all three quality dimensions (109/(LPIPS×#​G)10^{9}/(\text{LPIPS}\times\#\text{G}), PSNR/#​G\text{PSNR}/\#\text{G}, SSIM/#​G\text{SSIM}/\#\text{G}), on which LinearMask-GS achieves the highest score against the 3DGS and LP-3DGS reference rows; a per-scene LPIPS-vs-#G visualization is provided in Sec. 5 of the supplementary material.

Tanks & Temples and Deep Blending.

On the Tanks & Temples and Deep Blending benchmarks, LinearMask-GS★ (FastGS-backbone variant that substitutes FastGS’s post-densification VCP module with our learned mask) reaches 24.18 dB PSNR and 0.825 SSIM with 0.29M Gaussians on Tanks & Temples, and 30.11 dB PSNR and 0.899 SSIM with 0.29M Gaussians on Deep Blending. This places LinearMask-GS★ in the sub-million primitive regime of recent fast-training baselines while achieving the best PSNR on Tanks & Temples average (24.18 dB), Dr Johnson (29.67 dB), and Deep Blending average (30.11 dB), surpassing FastGS and other fast-training methods on these metrics. The supplementary material provides the full quantitative comparison against recent fast-training and compact 3DGS baselines, together with per-scene score tables for both benchmarks.

Qualitative comparison.

Figure 2 shows per-pixel absolute error maps for three representative Mip-NeRF 360 scenes (Bicycle, Flowers, Counter); error maps for the remaining six scenes are provided in the supplementary material. For each scene, error maps are visualized under a scene-specific colormap (blue to red indicates low to high absolute error), and per-image PSNR and MAE are reported below each panel. Across all nine scenes, LinearMask-GS produces lower MAE and fewer saturated high-error (red) regions than both LP-3DGS and 3DGS. The improvement is most visible in texture-dense outdoor scenes such as Flowers and Stump, where 3DGS error maps show large red areas around the foliage and 3DGS PSNR drops to 20.19 and 24.94 dB respectively, while LinearMask-GS retains 23.49 and 27.07 dB with substantially cleaner error maps. In indoor scenes such as Counter and Kitchen, the per-image PSNR margin over 3DGS exceeds 2.7 dB, reflecting more accurate reconstruction of fine structures like the countertop and the toy loader despite using fewer Gaussians overall (Table 1).

Training time.

Table 2 reports mean training time over the nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, all measured on a single RTX 4090. On the 3DGS backbone, LinearMask-GS is 2.12 minutes faster than its learned-mask parent LP-3DGS while reaching a much more compact final model with higher PSNR and SSIM (0.94M vs. 1.48M Gaussians, Table 1), and incurs only a 0.9-minute overhead over the unpruned 3DGS baseline despite the added mask-training and fine-tuning stages. On the FastGS backbone, LinearMask-GS★ reduces training time (1.93 to 1.81 minutes) while removing additional primitives: the brief mask-learning stage is more than offset by faster iterations on the already-pruned model, yielding a net saving; a full timing breakdown is provided in Sec. 13 of the supplementary material.

4.3 Generality across Backbones

2DGS.

We apply LinearMask-GS to the official 2DGS [Huang et al.(2024)Huang, Yu, Chen, Geiger, and Gao] codebase to test the generality of our framework across different Gaussian representations. While 3DGS and 2DGS utilize different geometric primitives, they share a consistent alpha-compositing pipeline, allowing our max-pooling score and linear activation to be applied without structural changes.

As shown in Table 3, on the nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes LinearMask-GS reduces the 2DGS Gaussian count by 2.9×2.9\times (from 1.06M to 0.36M) while improving PSNR by 0.22 dB and SSIM by 0.009, with LPIPS rising only marginally (by 0.008). This indicates that our importance masking successfully identifies redundant 2D disks without sacrificing perceptual quality.

DropGaussian and Octree-GS.

Beyond 2DGS, we further test LinearMask-GS on two additional Gaussian-based backbones with different representational structures: DropGaussian [Park et al.(2025)Park, Ryu, and Kim], which regularizes 3D Gaussians through stochastic dropout, and Octree-GS [Ren et al.(2024)Ren, Jiang, Lu, Yu, Xu, Ni, and Dai], which uses hierarchical anchor structures. On DropGaussian, we evaluate five LLFF scenes (9-view) with the masked model repeated over three independent training runs. Averaged over the runs, LinearMask-GS improves PSNR on every scene, by +0.31+0.31 to +0.52+0.52 dB over the unpruned backbone, while retaining 41%41\% fewer primitives than the Gumbel variant (per-scene results in Sec. 12 of the supplementary material). The single fern run of Table 3 gives a smaller gain (+0.03+0.03 dB at a 2.8×2.8\times reduction), indicating that single runs of this sparse-view backbone are noisy. On Octree-GS, the amsterdam scene from Bungee-NeRF shows a 2.9×2.9\times anchor reduction (1.09M to 0.38M) with +0.12+0.12 dB PSNR and SSIM/LPIPS within 0.0020.002 of the reference; on the bicycle and garden scenes of Mip-NeRF 360, anchors drop by 40.2%40.2\% relative to the Gumbel variant at a mean PSNR change of −0.11-0.11 dB. Across all three Octree-GS scenes, quality thus moves by at most ≈\approx0.1 dB in either direction while anchors are reduced by 40%40\% or more. Table 3 consolidates these results alongside the 2DGS comparison, and additionally reports the 2DGS variant with the linear-increment activation replaced by Gumbel-Sigmoid; the activation-level comparison across backbones is analyzed in Sec. 4.4.

4.4 Ablation Study

We ablate the core design choices of LinearMask-GS on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset: the importance aggregation, the mask activation, and the minimum-survival ratio ρ\rho. Unless stated otherwise, all variants use the default configuration: λm=5×10−4\lambda_{m}=5\times 10^{-4}, τ=0.1\tau=0.1, and ρ=0.30\rho=0.30. Detailed analyses of training convergence and additional hyperparameter sensitivity (sparsity weight λm\lambda_{m} and slope τ\tau) are provided in the supplementary material.

Aggregation and activation.

Table 4 presents a full factorial comparison of summation-based [Fang and Wang(2024)] and max-pooling [Niemeyer et al.(2025)Niemeyer, Manhardt, Rakotosaona, Oechsle, Duckworth, Gosula, Tateno, Bates, Kaeser, and Tombari] aggregation against Gumbel-Sigmoid [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan] and linear increment activations. Note that the “Max + Gumbel-Sigmoid” variant corresponds exactly to the LP-3DGS baseline reported in Table 1. For the summation-based variants (rows 1–2), we use ρ=0.40\rho=0.40 following the pruning statistics of LP-3DGS [Zhang et al.(2024)Zhang, Song, Lee, Yang, Peng, Chellappa, and Fan]; max-pooling variants use the default ρ=0.30\rho=0.30. Under max-pooling, replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with the linear increment activation reduces the Gaussian count from 1.48M to 0.94M and improves both PSNR (27.47 to 27.70 dB) and LPIPS (0.2258 to 0.2095). Under summation, the linear-increment variant reduces the count from 1.43M to 1.26M with nearly identical PSNR/LPIPS, indicating that the view-count inflation introduced by summation aggregation dominates the effect of the activation choice and obscures the stability benefit that Linear provides. The combination of max-pooling aggregation and the linear-increment activation gives the best operating point and is used in LinearMask-GS.

Ranking reliability.

The premise of top-ρ​N\rho N pruning is that the ranking induced by ψi\psi_{i} tracks importance, so we test this directly: with hard pruning disabled, the mask ranking through the window is compared against a held-out proxy, the max-pooled contribution of each Gaussian (Eq. (4)) at iteration 30k (protocol in Sec. 3 of the supplementary material). Across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, at the pruning decision point: (i) re-sampling the Gumbel noise alone flips 47.3%47.3\% of keep/prune decisions (4646–48%48\% on every scene; rank correlation between two noise draws < 0.1{<}\,0.1), so the sampled decision is governed by activation noise rather than by a stable learned ranking, whereas the linear mask is deterministic (0%0\% flips); (ii) 52.2%52.2\% of Gumbel-Sigmoid mask values are saturated under this protocol versus 0.00%0.00\% for linear, consistent with the 51.19%51.19\% observed under the standard schedule (Sec. 3.3); (iii) the Spearman correlation between the mask ranking and the proxy is 0.290.29 for linear versus 0.160.16 for Gumbel-Sigmoid (1.8×1.8\times higher overall and 2.8×2.8\times on outdoor scenes; per-iteration curves in the supplementary material).

Contribution of the learned mask.

To isolate what the mask adds over its ingredients, we also prune directly by the raw score: same schedule, top-30%30\% by SiS_{i} at 20k, then identical fine-tuning (“Max + none” in Table 4). This mask-free baseline is strong (27.5727.57 dB / 0.82310.8231 / 0.21430.2143 at 0.960.96M), yet our learned mask is ahead on eight of the nine scenes at a smaller budget (+0.13+0.13 dB at 0.940.94M; the only exception is Treehill; per-scene results in Sec. 10 of the supplement). The Gumbel-Sigmoid mask falls below it (27.4727.47 dB, 1.481.48M): once the ranking saturates, a learned mask is worse than none. With the ranking-reliability analysis above, this locates the gain: not max-pooling or fine-tuning, both shared with these baselines, but the stability of the ranking itself.

Minimum-survival ratio ρ\rho.

We sweep ρ∈{0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50}\rho\in\{0.10,\,0.20,\,0.30,\,0.40,\,0.50\} on all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes for both the linear-increment activation and the matched Gumbel-Sigmoid baseline under the identical top-ρ​N\rho N rule of Eq. (9) (Secs. 8–9 of the supplementary material). Two observations follow. First, the two quality–compression curves share the same shape: quality improves steeply up to ρ=0.30\rho{=}0.30 and largely saturates beyond it (over ρ=0.30→0.50\rho{=}0.30{\to}0.50, PSNR gains total +0.04+0.04 dB for linear and +0.11+0.11 dB for Gumbel-Sigmoid). Within the linear sweep, ρ=0.20\rho{=}0.20 removes too many meaningful primitives (−0.28-0.28 dB), whereas ρ=0.40\rho{=}0.40 retains 34%34\% more Gaussians for only +0.03+0.03 dB, so we keep ρ=0.30\rho{=}0.30 as the default. Second, the curves differ in position: because top-ρ​N\rho N retains the same fraction of a near-identical primitive pool, equal ρ\rho implies matched budgets (#G differs by ≤0.01\leq 0.01M), and at every ρ\rho the linear-increment activation sits +0.40+0.40–0.480.48 dB above the Gumbel-Sigmoid baseline at the same budget. The gap does not close anywhere on the sweep: the baseline’s best point (27.3327.33 dB at ρ=0.50\rho{=}0.50, 1.571.57M) falls below even the linear ρ=0.20\rho{=}0.20 setting (27.4227.42 dB at 0.630.63M, 2.5×2.5\times fewer primitives) and never reaches our default (27.7027.70 dB at 0.940.94M) despite 67%67\% more primitives. The stable ranking thus does not reshape the trade-off; it selects a better subset at every budget, shifting the entire curve.

Activation choice across backbones.

The factorial ablation above is conducted on the 3DGS backbone. To verify that the activation itself, rather than the masking framework, drives the gain, we compare the two activations on DropGaussian and Octree-GS with the mask window, sparsity loss, importance score, and target keep ratio held identical (the “+ LP-3DGS (Gumbel)” vs. “+ LinearMask-GS” rows of Table 3). The linear-increment activation prunes 40%40\% (DropGaussian, fern) and 41%41\% (Octree-GS, amsterdam) further than the Gumbel-Sigmoid variant while maintaining or improving quality; since these backbones use markedly different mask-training schedules (1,500 and 4,000 iterations), the activation choice, not merely the masking framework, governs the achievable quality–compression trade-off.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we identified a limitation of existing learned-mask pruning for 3D Gaussian Splatting and introduced LinearMask-GS to address it. The steep slope of Gumbel-Sigmoid pushes mask values to 00 or 11 before the importance ranking stabilizes, a failure that longer mask-training windows exacerbate rather than fix, producing a two-peaked distribution from which that ranking can no longer be reliably recovered. Replacing it with a linear-increment activation keeps mask values in the mid-confidence regime and preserves their ranking, so a simple top-ρ​N\rho N selection suffices, and this single change transfers without modification across diverse Gaussian-based backbones.

Limitations.

The slope τ\tau and ratio ρ\rho are tuned on a held-out set (Sec. 4.1) and fixed across scenes; the brief mask window can leave specular or transparent regions under-discriminated, and the global ρ\rho sets an overall rather than per-region budget. The method also inherits the static-scene assumption of its backbones; scene-adaptive scheduling and dynamic-scene extensions are left for future work.
